items.title: 13.5 Reactions of the halogens with hydrogen

blocks.text: Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides, H2 + X2 gives 2HX (X2 = F2, Cl2, Br2, I2); hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids. The reactivity with hydrogen decreases from fluorine to iodine. Fluorine reacts explosively with hydrogen even at low temperature and in the dark, H2 + F2 gives 2HF, which dissolves in water as hydrofluoric acid. In UV light or with a spark chlorine reacts readily with hydrogen to give colourless HCl gas, which forms hydrochloric acid in water. Hydrogen bromide is produced when bromine reacts with hydrogen on heating, an exothermic reaction; HBr is less reactive than HCl and HF and forms strong hydrobromic acid in water. At high temperature with a catalyst iodine reacts with hydrogen to give hydrogen iodide, which forms hydroiodic acid in water; this reaction is reversible and very slow.

blocks.alt: Top left: a table of the conditions for hydrogen reacting with each halogen, from explosive in the dark for fluorine to slow and reversible with a catalyst for iodine. Top right: a bar chart of H-X bond energies 569, 431, 366 and 299 kJ mol-1 with the stability order. Bottom left: the reducing power order of the halide ions with reasons. Bottom right: a table of what happens when sodium halides meet concentrated sulfuric acid, with the balanced equations.
blocks.caption: Reactions of halogens with hydrogen, thermal stability of the hydrogen halides, halide ions as reducing agents, and halides with concentrated sulfuric acid (original diagram after topics 13.5 to 13.9 and Table 13.5).
blocks.long_description: Hydrogen combines explosively with fluorine in the dark, readily with chlorine in light, on heating with bromine, and only slowly and reversibly with iodine over a catalyst. The hydrogen halides formed are stable in proportion to their bond energies, which fall from hydrogen fluoride to hydrogen iodide as the halogen atom grows and overlaps less well with hydrogen, so hydrogen iodide decomposes most easily on heating. The halide ions reverse the halogen trend: iodide, large and of low charge density, gives up its electron most readily and is the strongest reducing agent, fluoride the weakest. With concentrated sulfuric acid, fluoride and chloride simply release the hydrogen halide, bromide also reduces the acid to sulfur dioxide and gives brown bromine, and iodide reduces it all the way to hydrogen sulfide and gives purple iodine.

blocks.text: The reaction between H2 and F2 is explosive but that between H2 and I2 is slow and reversible. Explain.
